q7.answer: Transaction C does it in one database transaction: moves the pending secret to the active secret and sets confirmed_at to now, deletes all old recovery codes and inserts 10 new hashed ones, sets last_step to the accepted step, and deletes every other session of the user (current one stays). If it fails partway, nothing changes: old secret, codes and sessions stay as they were. It applies only if the pending secret is still present and unexpired.

q8.answer: It is the Challenge, a login_challenges(token_hash, user_id, expires_at, failures) row, deliberately not a sessions row. The browser holds the raw token in a short-lived mfa cookie (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, max-age 5 minutes); only its hash is stored. It is removed on success, on the 5th wrong entry, or on expiry (checked on use, with a periodic cleanup job only to keep the table small).

q9.answer: The sealed secret is in user_totp.secret_sealed, the pending one in pending_secret_sealed and pending_expires_at, the replay guard in user_totp.last_step, and recovery codes as hashes in recovery_codes(user_id, code_hash, used_at). 2FA is on only when confirmed_at in user_totp is not null.

q10.answer: The old secret stays untouched in secret_sealed, and the old recovery codes stay valid, so sign-in keeps using the old authenticator and never reads the pending secret. If the replacement is abandoned or expires, nothing changes: the pending secret counts as absent and the old authenticator keeps working. Starting again overwrites the pending secret.

q11.answer: One field: exactly 6 digits is an authenticator code, anything else is a recovery code (recovery codes are 10 characters like abcde-fghij, never 6 digits). Yes, any wrong entry, including an unknown recovery code, adds a row to the per-user wrong-entry log and increments the challenge's failures; the 5th wrong entry deletes the challenge.
